tweets: Alexander's army marched out of India in 325 BCE. His sculptors' style stayed behind - and ended up carving the face of the Buddha.
For centuries after the Buddha's death, artists refused to show his face at all - only a footprint, an empty throne, a wheel. Then something changed in a frontier region called Gandhara.

Greek colonists settled there after Alexander's campaigns. Under the later Kushan Empire (1st-3rd century CE), their descendants began sculpting the Buddha in a Greek toga-like robe, with wavy Apollo curls and a serene Hellenistic face.
This Greco-Buddhist style - Gandhara art - spread along Silk Road trade routes into Central Asia, China, and Japan, shaping how Buddha images look to this day.

A conqueror's armies left India within a few years. His sculptors' style still shapes how a billion people picture the Buddha, 2,300 years on. 🗿 Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
